extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of poetry; literary critics and general readers seeking guidance on judging poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to read, judge, and appreciate poetry: distinguishing genuine poetic excellence from historic or personal bias, using masters as touchstones, and assessing both matter and manner (truth/seriousness; diction/movement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude charlatanism / preserve critical distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry ... it is the glory, the eternal honor, that charlatanism shall find no entrance; that this noble sphere be kept inviolate and inviolable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charlatanism means confusing or obliterating the distinctions between excellent and inferior, sound and unsound, true and untrue. It is unpermissible in poetry to confuse these distinctions; critics and readers must maintain clear discriminations of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a constant 'sense for the best' (the real estimate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes; constantly in reading poetry, a sense for the best, the really excellent, and of the strength and joy to be drawn from it, should be present in our minds and should govern our estimate of what we read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set the aim of finding and enjoying the best poetry fixedly before your mind; continually revert to that standard while reading to avoid distraction by lesser aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the historic estimate fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet or a poem may count to us historically ... we may easily bring ourselves to make it of more importance as poetry than in itself it really is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let a poem's historical role or position in development substitute for judgment of its intrinsic poetic quality. Historic interest can mislead critics into over-rating a work as 'classic' when its poetic merits are lesser (examples: comparing Cædmon to Milton; overrating medieval romance-poetry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the personal estimate fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet or a poem may count to us on grounds personal to ourselves ... Our personal affinities, likings, and circumstances, have great power to sway our estimate ... and to make us attach more importance to it as poetry than in itself it really possesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be vigilant about personal biases and affinities that cause over-rating; separate what matters to you personally from what is genuinely excellent as poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the masters as concrete touchstones
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no more useful help ... than to have always in one's mind lines and expressions of the great masters, and to apply them as a touchstone to other poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorize and internalize short passages or lines from the greatest poets (Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, Milton, etc.) to test other poetry by direct comparison of felt quality, rather than relying solely on abstract definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concrete exemplars over abstract character lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics give themselves great labor to draw out what in the abstract constitutes the characters of a high quality of poetry. It is much better simply to have recourse to concrete examples ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn poetic quality by feeling it in master verses rather than by reading theoretical lists; when forced to abstract, restrict claims to where qualities arise (matter and manner) but privilege experiential recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess both substance (matter) and manner (style)
rubrics_metrics.description: They are in the matter and substance of the poetry, and they are in its manner and style. Both of these, the substance and matter on the one hand, the style and manner on the other, have a mark, an accent, of high beauty, worth, and power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a poem's content (truth, seriousness, insight) and its stylistic execution (diction, movement) separately and together; both contribute to high poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance: poetic truth and high seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance and matter of the best poetry acquire their special character from possessing, in an eminent degree, truth and seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to whether the poem offers a high criticism of life — depth, truthfulness, and serious purpose — as a core criterion of excellence (examples: Homer, Dante, Shakespeare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner: excellence of diction and movement
rubrics_metrics.description: To the style and manner of the best poetry their special character, their accent, is given by their diction, and, even yet more, by their movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the poem's verbal choices and especially rhythmic/musical movement; superior diction and movement are distinguishing marks of great poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of matter and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: The two superiorities are closely related, and are in steadfast proportion one to the other. So far as high poetic truth and seriousness are wanting to a poet's matter and substance, so far also, we may be sure, will a high poetic stamp of diction and movement be wanting to his style and manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect substance and style to co-vary: absence of deep truth/seriousness usually coincides with absence of high diction/movement; evaluate how they support each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate technical versification with true poetic greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation may have versifiers with smooth numbers and easy rhymes, and yet may have no real poetry at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that mastery of meter/rhyme/technical regularity (versification) is not sufficient for being a poetic classic; look for the deeper qualities (truth, seriousness, diction/movement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of scholarly overpreparation that impedes enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: The elaborate philological groundwork ... goes on, but the authors are little known and less enjoyed. So with the investigator of 'historic origins' in poetry ... he often is distracted from the enjoyment of the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting historical/philological study become an end that obscures the primary aim: enjoying and appreciating the best poetry. Scholarship should serve, not replace, sensibility to poetic excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the real estimate even when historical/contextual excuses exist
rubrics_metrics.description: We are to adopt a real, not a historic, estimate of poetry. ... To trace the labor, the attempts, the weaknesses, the failures of a genuine classic ... is mere literary dilettantism unless it has that clear sense and deeper enjoyment for its end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a poet, consider historical limitations and origins but ultimately rank works by their intrinsic excellence and capacity to produce deep enjoyment; historical study is valuable only insofar as it enhances real appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate genuine classics from false/dubious classics
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything depends on the reality of a poet's classic character. If he is a dubious classic, let us sift him; if he is a false classic, let us explode him. But if he is a real classic ... the great thing for us is to feel and enjoy his work as deeply as ever we can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of 'classic' status critically: test whether a poet's work actually belongs to the class of the very best and respond accordingly—engage and enjoy true classics; scrutinize or reject false ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of criticism: form and deepen appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: A clearer, deeper sense of the best is the most precious benefit which we can gather from a poetical collection ... we should therefore steadily set it before our minds at the outset, and should compel ourselves to revert constantly to the thought of it as we proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use criticism as a formative practice whose aim is to cultivate readers' ability to recognize and enjoy the best poetry; prioritize formative ends over mere historical cataloging or personal preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cautious comparative judgment when praising works across orders
rubrics_metrics.description: If our words are to have any meaning, if our judgments are to have any solidity, we must not heap that supreme praise upon poetry of an order immeasurably inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing works from different poetic orders or traditions, avoid inflating praise for lesser-order pieces by inappropriate analogy to supreme masterpieces; retain precision in comparative valuation (example: Chanson de Roland vs Homer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that historical missions shape but do not define poetic excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The men of letters ... must of necessity give a predominating ... attention to the qualities of regularity, uniformity, precision, balance. But an almost exclusive attention to these qualities involves some repression and silencing of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that poets serving particular historical/cultural missions (e.g., founders of a 'fit prose' age) may excel in certain technical virtues appropriate to their time, but these mission-driven achievements should not be automatically equated with the highest poetic virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate that linguistic liberties don't substitute for talent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often said that the power of liquidness and fluidity in Chaucer's verse was dependent upon a free ... dealing with language ... It is true that Chaucer's fluidity is conjoined with this liberty, and is admirably served by it; but we ought not to say that it was dependent upon it. It was dependent upon his talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing fluid diction or movement, attribute them primarily to poetic talent rather than merely to period-specific linguistic freedoms; other talented poets can achieve similar effects without the same liberties.
